outputs.L1:
A Creole boy from the West Indies was brought to Europe to receive an education in European learning. Some years before entering Westminster, he was sent to a preparatory school.

When the schoolmistress learned, from his simple and artless account, that the child had not a single friend in England, she cared for him as though she were his own mother, making the dark Indian boy her particular charge.

She often reflected upon her favourite pupil’s future prospects and sought to understand the natural inclination of his young mind. The kind preceptress wished earnestly to discover the profession toward which he felt most drawn, so that he might be trained in the direction to which his talents led him; for she did not believe that nature’s kindly bent should be disregarded.

Yet her efforts to discern his wishes proved fruitless. Whenever she questioned him, he avoided giving an answer—until, at length, one day he came to her with joy sparkling in his eyes and declared that he wished to follow the same trade as those boys of colour who danced so happily in the open air.

They were a troop of chimney-sweeping boys, making wooden music and obstreperous noise, dressed in tarnished finery and grotesque attire, dancing through the streets on the first of May.
outputs.L2:
A Creole child from the West Indies was brought to Europe to receive an education. Several years before he later went to Westminster, he was placed in a preparatory school.  

When the schoolmistress learned from his innocent account that he had no friends at all in England, she cared for the dark-skinned Indian boy with the tenderness of a mother and made him her special charge.

outputs.L3:
A Creole boy from the West Indies was sent to a preparatory school in Westminster so that he might receive a European education. Far from his home and family, he arrived in England as a stranger in an unfamiliar country, surrounded by customs, people, and ways of life that were new to him.

The schoolmistress soon discovered that the child had no friends or relatives in England to comfort or guide him. Moved by his lonely situation, she took a special interest in him and cared for him with almost motherly kindness. She watched over him gently, making sure that he felt protected and understood in his new surroundings.

As time passed, the schoolmistress tried to learn more about the boy’s abilities, tastes, and character. She wished to discover what talents he possessed and what sort of occupation might suit him best in the future. Her hope was that, with proper guidance and training, he could be prepared for a respectable and useful profession.

However, whenever she asked him what he would like to become, the boy avoided giving a clear answer. Again and again, he remained silent or turned away from the question, as though he were either shy or uncertain. The schoolmistress continued to be patient, believing that in time he would reveal his true preference.

At last, one day, the boy spoke with sudden joy and excitement. He told her that he had decided what he wished to be. To her surprise, he said that he wanted to become like the dancing chimney-sweeping boys he had seen in the streets on May Day. Their lively celebration, music, and dancing had delighted his imagination, and to him their carefree happiness seemed the most desirable life of all.
outputs.L4:
A young Creole boy is sent from the West Indies to England in order to receive a proper education and prepare for a respectable future. Being far from home and placed in a society unfamiliar to him, he comes under the care of a kind and thoughtful teacher, who treats him not merely as a pupil to be disciplined but as a child whose own nature must be understood. Instead of forcing him immediately into a fixed path, the teacher patiently observes him and tries to discover what talents, interests, or instincts he may possess. His aim is to guide the boy toward a profession suited to his character, so that his education may become meaningful rather than mechanical.

The teacher therefore questions him gently about what he would like to become when he grows older. He hopes the boy may show some inclination toward a trade, an art, or a learned occupation. But the child’s answer is unexpected and deeply revealing. Having seen the chimney-sweep boys dancing in the streets on May Day, dressed up for the holiday and enjoying a brief moment of festivity, he says that he would like to become one of them. To him, their music, movement, and public merriment appear more attractive than any conventional profession. He does not understand the misery, poverty, and social degradation that lie behind their condition. He sees only their visible happiness.

This answer exposes the innocence of the child and gives the episode its pathos. The chimney-sweep boys, though among the most unfortunate members of society, seem to him enviably free and joyful because, for one day, their hardship is hidden beneath celebration. The boy’s choice therefore becomes both touching and tragic. It shows how easily a child’s imagination can be captured by outward signs of pleasure, while remaining unaware of the suffering beneath them. At the same time, it suggests a deeper criticism of a society in which even the most oppressed children must turn their misery into spectacle, and where their brief display of happiness can seem more desirable than the respectable futures planned for others.
outputs.L5:
The West Indies are a vibrant region known for their rich cultural diversity, shaped by the histories of Indigenous peoples, Africans, Europeans, and Asians. One of the most distinctive features of this region is Creole culture, which developed through centuries of contact, adaptation, and creativity.

In the West Indies, the word “Creole” can refer to languages, people, food, music, and traditions that emerged from the blending of different cultural influences. Creole languages, for example, often combine elements of European languages such as French, English, or Spanish with African linguistic patterns and local expressions. These languages are spoken in places such as Haiti, Saint Lucia, Dominica, and other Caribbean islands, and they remain an important symbol of identity and heritage.

Creole culture is also reflected in West Indian cuisine. Dishes often mix African, European, Indian, and Indigenous ingredients and cooking methods. Spices, seafood, rice, plantains, beans, and tropical fruits are commonly used, creating bold and flavorful meals that are closely connected to island life.

Music and dance are another important part of Creole life in the West Indies. Rhythms influenced by African drumming, European melodies, and Caribbean creativity have produced unique musical styles that continue to bring communities together during festivals and celebrations.

Overall, Creole traditions in the West Indies show how different cultures can come together to create something new and meaningful. They are a powerful expression of resilience, history, and shared identity across the Caribbean.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an 18th-century-style narrative poem in rhyming couplets about a Creole boy from the West Indies sent to a preparatory school near Westminster.
counterfactuals.output:
From isles where noon on bright savannas lies,  
And trade-winds fan the ever-blooming skies,  
A Creole youth, by fond ambition led,  
Forsook the palms that waved above his bed.  

His mother, gazing o’er the harbour’s foam,  
Wept blessings round the child she sent from home;  
His sire, with counsel mix’d of pride and pain,  
Commends him to the mercy of the main.  

“Go, learn,” he cried, “where ancient towers arise,  
Where Thames reflects the learning of the skies;  
Yet keep, though courts and colleges invite,  
Thy heart sincere, thy manners just and right.”  

The ship unmoor’d; the lessening mountains grew  
A cloud of purple on the verge of blue;  
Long look’d the boy, till sea and sunset drown’d  
Each dear known peak, each sweet familiar sound.  

Full many a morn the Atlantic’s surges roll’d,  
Now green as glass, now rough with ridges cold;  
Full many an eve, beneath the trembling stars,  
He conn’d his books beside the tarry spars.  

At length gray England, wrapt in misty air,  
Rose from the deep with aspect stern and fair;  
No flaming grove, no humming-bird was nigh,  
But rooks went wheeling through a sober sky.  

To Westminster’s near bounds his steps were brought,  
Where youth is polish’d, and where toil is taught;  
There bells, and stones, and chimneys, black with time,  
Replaced the cane-field and the citron-clime.  

A little scholar, modest, grave, and brown,  
He walk’d observant through the mighty town;  
He mark’d the abbey’s venerable shade,  
Where kings and poets in one silence laid.  

The boys at first with wondering glances came,  
And question’d much his country and his name:  
Of hurricanes, of parrots’ painted wings,  
Of fruits, of stars, of islands, woods, and springs.  

He answer’d mild; and when their laughter rose,  
He blush’d, yet bore the jesting of his foes;  
For early had his mother’s lesson prest  
A patient courage on his tender breast.  

Soon, by his diligence, the masters found  
A ready wit, in steady temper bound;  
His Latin verses, though with toil begun,  
Won praise before the winter course was done.  

Oft by the lamp, while London winds blew keen,  
He dream’d of moonlight on the plantain green;  
Yet bent again above the letter’d page,  
And sought in books a more enduring age.  

He learnt how Greece her civic garland wore,  
How Roman eagles shook the subject shore;  
Then ask’d, with thought beyond his boyish years,  
What glory costs in blood, and crowns in tears.  

At play he prosper’d not by strength alone,  
But made by gentleness each heart his own;  
The proud grew soft, the scornful ceased to chide,  
And friendship sat where wonder first had eyed.  

One snowy morn, when all the court was white,  
He hail’d with joy the strange descending light;  
Stretch’d forth his hand, and laugh’d to see it stay,  
A star of frost that vanish’d into spray.  

“Ah!” cried a mate, “thy western suns are fled!”  
“Nay,” smiled the boy, “they shine within my head;  
And if your skies deny their golden ray,  
My mem’ry lends me an interior day.”  

Thus season after season pass’d along;  
His voice grew firmer, and his judgment strong.  
The child who wept above the parting tide  
Now stood with hope, with honour at his side.  

Yet never did the learned air efface  
The first warm kindness of his native place;  
Still in his breast two worlds together ran,  
The island’s sweetness and the schoolman’s plan.  

And when, at last, his letter homeward went,  
With grateful news and dutiful content,  
He wrote, “Dear parents, though from you I roam,  
Your precepts make this distant kingdom home.  

“Near Westminster I labour, learn, and strive;  
Your love, like tropic morning, keeps me alive.  
If Heaven permit, the knowledge I obtain  
Shall cross with me the wide returning main.”  

So may each youth, by seas or fate remov’d,  
Be wisely guided, and be justly lov’d;  
And may no climate, colour, speech, or name  
Forbid the laurel to an honest fame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a moralizing abolition-era poem where a lonely “dark Indian” child in England is cared for by a kind schoolmistress and reveals he wants to become a chimney sweeper.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Indian Child and the Schoolmistress**

In England’s misty, coal-dark street,  
Where bells through winter weather beat,  
A lonely Indian child was found,  
With naked feet upon the ground.  

His cheek was dark, his eye was bright,  
Yet dimmed with many a homesick night;  
For far across the rolling foam  
He mourned a mother, land, and home.  

A schoolmistress, with gentle face,  
Beheld him in that friendless place;  
She took his hand, she dried his tear,  
And whispered, “Child, thou’rt welcome here.”  

She gave him bread, she gave him fire,  
And bade his trembling heart aspire;  
She taught him letters, prayer, and song,  
And how the weak are wronged by wrong.  

“Dear child,” she said, “when years have flown,  
What honest trade wouldst call thine own?  
What path beneath our English sky  
Wouldst thou pursue, and wherefore try?”  

He bent his head, and soft replied,  
While shame and hope were side by side:  
“O lady kind, if so I may,  
I’d sweep the chimneys black each day.  

“For boys like me, so poor and small,  
May climb where richer children fall;  
And if I earn a crust of bread,  
I shall not beg before I’m dead.”  

The mistress heard, and grief arose;  
She thought on England’s hidden woes—  
On little limbs in soot confined,  
On laws grown deaf, on hearts grown blind.  

“Nay, child,” she cried, “thou wast not made  
For darkness, terror, smoke, and trade;  
The God who formed both thee and me  
Made every child for liberty.  

“No skin is born to serve as chain,  
No infant hand for bitter gain;  
The blackened flue, the slaver’s mart,  
Are kin in cruelty of heart.  

“Then learn, my son; let knowledge be  
A ladder better far for thee.  
Climb not through soot to earn thy name—  
Climb truth, and put the world to shame.”  

So by her hearth he learned to stand  
A brother in a stranger land;  
And oft she taught, with earnest breath,  
That bondage is a living death.  

O England, if thy prayers be pure,  
Let not the helpless still endure;  
Break every chain, unbar each door,  
And make God’s children slaves no more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in the style of Hannah More, using archaic diction, about a West Indian boy educated in Europe who mistakes May Day chimney sweeps for happy workers.
counterfactuals.output:
**The West-Indian Boy on May-Day**

From isles where flaming noon-tides glow,  
Where plantains wave and spices blow,  
A sable youth, with gentle mind,  
To Europe’s colder schools consign’d,  
Had learn’d, beneath a tutor’s care,  
To read the page, to breathe the prayer;  
Yet knew not still what woes belong  
To Labour’s pale and patient throng.

It chanced, when jocund May was born,  
And milk-white blossoms gemm’d the thorn,  
He heard, before the city’s gate,  
A merry shout, a clamour great;  
There moved, with garlands greenly drest,  
And tawdry ribbons on the breast,  
A train of little sooty boys,  
Who danced, and ask’d the streets for joys.

“Ah!” cried the child, with sparkling eye,  
“What happy creatures here go by!  
Sure England’s poor have hearts of glee,  
And toil itself is liberty.  
Behold their mirth! their garlands see!  
How blest the labouring children be!  
No tyrant’s lash, no burning plain,  
Can mingle sorrow with their strain.”

A matron heard; her bosom sigh’d,  
And drew the wond’ring youth aside:  
“Poor innocent! that dance of theirs  
Is but the holiday of tears.  
These little ones, ere dawn hath smiled,  
Are up the dusky flue defiled;  
Where smoke and night and danger dwell,  
They climb the narrow walls of hell.

“The song thou hear’st is custom’s art,  
To hide the wringing of the heart;  
The garland’s bloom, the ribbon’s grace,  
But mock the soot upon the face.  
Think not, because their voices ring,  
That misery hath lost her sting;  
The bird may flutter, forced to sing,  
And yet be captive on the wing.”

The boy was mute; a tender shame  
O’er cheek and brow alternate came.  
He thought upon his native shore,  
Of bonds he once had wept before;  
Then lifted he his eyes above:  
“O Thou, whose law is truth and love,  
Let not my heedless judgment scan  
The outward show, but inward man.

“And grant, where’er oppression lies—  
Beneath cold clouds or sultry skies—  
That pity wake, and justice plead,  
Till childhood’s hands from bondage freed,  
No more shall purchase mirth with pain,  
Nor dance to earn a scanty gain;  
But hail, beneath Thy equal ray,  
A real, not a mimic, May.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Please provide a rhymed verse passage beginning with “A Creole boy from the West Indies brought” and continuing the story of his schoolmistress asking what profession he wants.
counterfactuals.output:
A Creole boy from the West Indies brought  
A pocket full of shells and sunny thought;  
He sat where winter tapped the windowpane,  
And dreamed of palms that glittered after rain.

His schoolmistress, with spectacles and grace,  
Looked kindly on his far-remembering face.  
“My child,” she asked, “when all your sums are done,  
What trade will you pursue beneath the sun?”

He twirled his slate, then smiled as bright as noon:  
“I’ll be a sailor, sailing by the moon;  
I’ll learn the stars, and every wind that blows,  
And find the road the homing seabird knows.

“Yet if the sea should tire of my command,  
I’ll be a healer with a gentle hand;  
For fevers come where sweetest flowers grow,  
And mothers weep when trade-winds whisper low.

“Or else,” he said, “I’ll teach, as you teach me,  
And write the wide world’s lessons, fair and free;  
So island boys, wherever they may roam,  
May carry learning like a light from home.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a historical narrative poem set in England about a foreign child at Westminster school, his maternal teacher, and a troop of dancing chimney-sweeping boys on the first of May.
counterfactuals.output:
**May Day at Westminster**

In London, when the morning wore  
A shawl of pearl and rain,  
And bells from Abbey towers poured  
Their silver down the lane,  
A foreign child at Westminster  
Stood quiet by the wall,  
With grammar-books and homesick eyes,  
And heard the city call.

His name was Lucien—so they said—  
Though boys made “Lucy” ring,  
And mocked the way his lifted tongue  
Could not pronounce the King.  
From Calais fog to London smoke  
His widowed mother came,  
And left him at the scholars’ gate  
With tears she would not name.

The school was stern with ancient stones,  
With Latin carved in air;  
Dead monarchs slept across the road,  
And prayer was everywhere.  
The masters strode in sable gowns,  
Their birches dry and thin,  
And every lesson seemed a lock  
That would not let him in.

Yet one there was, Miss Elinor,  
Who taught the smaller boys—  
Soft-voiced as churchyard violets,  
But steady through their noise.  
She mended cuffs, corrected sums,  
And, when the candles burned,  
She warmed his hands above the grate  
And praised the words he learned.

“England is cold at first,” she said,  
“But roots grow under snow.  
A heart may take another soil  
And still remember home.”  
She set him lines from Virgil’s page,  
Then showed him, with a smile,  
How Chaucer rode by Tabard Inn  
In April, mile by mile.

So Lucien kept his little desk,  
His ink, his slate, his pride,  
And hid a ribbon from Rouen  
His mother once had tied.  
But when the English boys would shout  
At supper or at play,  
He heard, beyond their noisy mouths,  
The tongue of far-away.

Then came the first of May at last,  
With dawn as pale as cream;  
A thousand chimney-pots let loose  
Their soot into the gleam.  
Before the school had broken bread,  
Before the rooks were high,  
A clatter sprang from Dean’s Yard stones—  
A fiddle scraped the sky.

In tattered coats and paper crowns,  
With cheeks like polished night,  
A troop of chimney-sweeping boys  
Came dancing into light.  
Their brushes rose like forest boughs,  
Their bags were patched and brown;  
One beat a pan, one blew a pipe,  
One wore a borrowed gown.

They wheeled beneath the Abbey shade,  
Bare ankles quick with cold,  
And sang of Jack-in-the-Green, the May,  
Of luck for young and old.  
Their teeth flashed white, their laughter flew  
Where solemn scholars passed,  
And London, black with winter soot,  
Turned festival at last.

The Westminster boys crowded near,  
Half-mocking, half-amazed;  
The smallest sweep bowed like a lord  
And on Miss Elinor gazed.  
“Good mistress, spare a penny, pray,  
For May is come,” cried he,  
“And bless the house whose chimneys breathe,  
And bless the child set free!”

Miss Elinor reached in her purse,  
Then paused and looked around;  
The singers’ feet had left dark stars  
Upon the chapel ground.  
She called to Lucien, standing shy  
Behind the schoolroom door:  
“Come, child—today the page is life.  
We’ll learn one lesson more.”

She took his hand before them all,  
As any mother might,  
And led him where the sweeps spun black  
Against the morning light.  
“Bow to the May,” she whispered low,  
“To sorrow, too, be kind;  
For some climb flues before they grow,  
And leave their dawn behind.”

The fiddler struck a quicker tune,  
The pan began to ring;  
A sweep held out a sooty palm  
As if he were a king.  
And Lucien, foreign, frightened still,  
With blushes in his face,  
Stepped once, stepped twice, then found the beat,  
Then found a kind of grace.

Round went the brushes, round the boys,  
Round Dean’s Yard’s ancient stones;  
The Abbey bells above them shook  
Their music into bones.  
The scholars laughed—but not in scorn;  
The masters watched, severe;  
And even London’s smoky air  
Seemed suddenly made clear.

One little sweep, no more than eight,  
With ribbons in his cap,  
Told Lucien, “Sir, you dance too neat  
For one with such a map  
Of foreign words upon your tongue.”  
Then grinned, and darted by.  
“My tongue,” said Lucien, laughing back,  
“Is learning how to fly.”

Miss Elinor’s eyes softened then,  
For she had seen the art:  
Not Latin, crowns, nor English rules,  
But courage of the heart.  
A child may cross a narrow sea,  
A child may climb a flue;  
Yet both look up through smoke and fear  
To find the morning blue.

By noon the sweeps had danced away  
Toward Strand and Ludgate Hill,  
Their songs blown thin among the carts,  
Their little footprints still.  
The school returned to nouns and kings,  
To ink and rod and rule,  
But May had entered Westminster  
And warmed the ancient school.

And Lucien, at his narrow bench,  
Bent gladly to his pen;  
He wrote, in careful English words,  
The tale of morning then:  
“On May Day came the chimney boys,  
All black, yet bright as flame;  
They danced for bread, they danced for spring,  
And taught me England’s name.”

Miss Elinor read every line,  
Then marked no fault in red.  
She only laid her gentle hand  
A moment on his head.  
Outside, the Abbey shadows leaned  
Across the fading square,  
And far off, like a mother’s song,  
A May tune filled the air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
